9	We observe this phenomenon at scale: across trajectories from two architecturally distinct agents---SWE-Agent \citep{yang2024sweagent} and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands}---on SWE-bench tasks \citep{jimenez2024swebench}, 28.5\% and 21.45\% of sliding windows exhibit stagnation under our silver labeling scheme, respectively, confirming that the failure mode is both prevalent and highly agent-dependent.
10

12	First, \emph{repetition detectors} such as cycle detection \citep{george2025cycledetection} and SpecRA \citep{pipis2025reasoningloop} identify structural repetition---exact or near-exact loops in action sequences---but by design miss semantically diverse stagnation where the agent varies its surface behavior while remaining functionally stuck.

16	More fundamentally, none of these approaches asks the prior question: \emph{what signals actually carry stagnation information?}
17	No systematic study has investigated whether detecting subtle agent failure requires sophisticated semantic understanding or whether simpler structural patterns suffice.
18	
19	We address this question through a systematic empirical study (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
20	Using a weak supervision framework \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming,ratner2017snorkel}, we construct silver-labeled datasets from over 205K windows spanning SWE-Agent (54,809 windows, 28.5\% silver-labeled stagnation) and OpenHands (150,652 windows, 21.45\% stagnation).

40

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

LLM agents are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon software engineering tasks---resolving GitHub issues, debugging production systems, and iterating on multi-file codebases across dozens of editing rounds \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent,wang2025openhands}.
As these deployments scale, a critical failure mode has emerged that is qualitatively different from crashes or syntax errors: the agent \emph{stagnates}---continuing to produce actions that appear purposeful while making no meaningful progress toward the task goal.
\citet{orlanski2026slopcodebench} document this degradation on SlopCodeBench, recording verbosity increases of 77\% and quality drops of 75.5\% in long-horizon coding trajectories, with no agent fully solving any benchmark problem end-to-end.
Crucially, the dominant failure pattern is not simple repetition but what we term \emph{semantic stagnation}: the agent issues varied commands, edits different files, and generates plausible-looking outputs, yet its behavior is functionally stuck.
This ``looks busy but going in circles'' pattern defeats existing monitoring tools, because surface-level action diversity masks the underlying lack of progress.
We observe this phenomenon at scale: across trajectories from two architecturally distinct agents---SWE-Agent \citep{yang2024sweagent} and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands}---on SWE-bench tasks \citep{jimenez2024swebench}, 28.5\% and 21.45\% of sliding windows exhibit stagnation under our silver labeling scheme, respectively, confirming that the failure mode is both prevalent and highly agent-dependent.

Existing approaches address aspects of this problem but fall short in three ways.
First, \emph{repetition detectors} such as cycle detection \citep{george2025cycledetection} and SpecRA \citep{pipis2025reasoningloop} identify structural repetition---exact or near-exact loops in action sequences---but by design miss semantically diverse stagnation where the agent varies its surface behavior while remaining functionally stuck.
Second, \emph{step-level scoring} via process reward models \citep{xi2025agentprm} evaluates individual actions in isolation, discarding the window-level temporal dynamics that distinguish transient setbacks from sustained stagnation---a distinction that requires reasoning over sequences of consecutive actions \citep{chen2025monitoring}.
A sequence of failed commands followed by a strategy switch, for instance, carries different diagnostic information than the same commands evaluated independently.
Third, \emph{LLM self-evaluation} \citep{shinn2023reflexion} is both expensive and fundamentally limited by the stuck model's own judgment; our LLM-as-judge baseline achieves only 0.6625 macro-F1 at \$11.66 per test set, well below lightweight feature-based alternatives.
More fundamentally, none of these approaches asks the prior question: \emph{what signals actually carry stagnation information?}
No systematic study has investigated whether detecting subtle agent failure requires sophisticated semantic understanding or whether simpler structural patterns suffice.

We address this question through a systematic empirical study (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
Using a weak supervision framework \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming,ratner2017snorkel}, we construct silver-labeled datasets from over 205K windows spanning SWE-Agent (54,809 windows, 28.5\% silver-labeled stagnation) and OpenHands (150,652 windows, 21.45\% stagnation).
Three labeling functions provide complementary noisy votes: command repetition ($\lambda_1$) targets repetitive behavior, file diff delta ($\lambda_2$) targets output productivity, and outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) propagates task-level outcomes backward through the trajectory.
Majority vote aggregation produces window-level binary labels with confidence scores.
Our window-level formulation ($k{=}5$ consecutive actions, stride 1) captures short-range temporal patterns---such as repeated failures followed by strategy changes---that step-level approaches cannot express, while providing the granularity to pinpoint \emph{when} stagnation begins and ends within a trajectory, enabling targeted interventions.
Against these silver labels, we systematically compare hand-crafted structural features, a neural embedding probe, and an LLM-as-judge baseline.

Our study yields three principal findings.

\textbf{Finding 1: Structural features dominate zero-shot cross-agent transfer.}
Thirty hand-crafted features---command repetition rates, file operation counts, edit distances---achieve 0.9951 macro-F1 in-domain (Random Forest) and 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1 (Gradient Boosting, SWE-Agent $\to$ OpenHands) with zero target data, outperforming the GRU embedding probe \citep{cho2014gru} zero-shot (0.598 on OpenHands, near chance) and the LLM-as-judge baseline (0.6625) by +36.9\,pp and +24.3\,pp, respectively.
However, the probe rapidly closes this gap with modest fine-tuning: 50\% target data reaches 0.968, within 2\,pp of the structural 0.967.
We note that in-domain evaluation uses silver labels (\S\ref{sec:circular}); cross-agent transfer and a pending gold set (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}) provide non-circular validation.
The structural advantage is encoder-agnostic: three embedding backbones \citep{zhang2025qwen3embedding} all yield probe F1 above 0.90, confirming that the probe's temporal architecture rather than a specific pretrained encoder drives performance.
The in-domain score of 0.9951 reflects circular evaluation---structural features overlap with LF inputs---but the cross-agent score of 0.967, where models trained on one agent's LF distribution are tested on another with substantially different firing patterns, breaks this circularity.
This finding challenges the prevailing intuition that detecting subtle agent failures requires complex language understanding, and suggests that lightweight structural monitoring---no GPU, under 5\,ms per window---may be more practical than neural or LLM-based approaches for real-time agent oversight.

\textbf{Finding 2: Labeling functions occupy agent-specific temporal niches.}
On SWE-Agent, command repetition ($\lambda_1$) leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps, file diff ($\lambda_2$) is near-concurrent at $-1.20$ steps, and outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) lags by 6.70 steps.
On OpenHands, $\lambda_1$ reverses from leading to lagging ($+3.32$ steps), where its 92.2\% stagnation-vote rate produces a 71\% false positive rate on progress windows.
Removing $\lambda_1$ from the OpenHands labeling pipeline improves fine-tuned probe F1 by 17.6\,pp, demonstrating that labeling functions validated on one agent architecture can become adversarial on another.

\textbf{Finding 3: Temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote.}
Three temporal label models---time-varying weights (TWV), Hidden Markov Models \citep{safranchik2020linkedhmm}, and lag-aware HMMs---all fail to surpass majority vote on downstream detection.
TWV achieves marginally higher self-evaluated F1 but degrades downstream probe performance by 2.57\,pp.
The root cause: three binary LFs produce too little inter-LF conflict for temporal aggregation to exploit.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Structural signal discovery.} We demonstrate that 30 lightweight structural features achieve near-perfect stagnation detection (0.9951 in-domain, 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1), outperforming neural probes and LLM judges by wide margins (+33.3\,pp over LLM-as-judge), with no GPU and under 5\,ms per window. This redirects agent monitoring from costly representation learning toward lightweight structural approaches.
    \item \textbf{Labeling function temporal dynamics.} We reveal that labeling functions occupy statistically distinct temporal niches relative to stagnation onset, with agent-specific reversals that corrupt silver labels when transferred across architectures, informing future weak-supervision design on sequential agent data.
    \item \textbf{Temporal label model negative finding.} We show that three temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote for downstream detection, despite clear temporal structure in LF firing patterns. This constrains future temporal label model research: the 3-LF regime produces insufficient conflict for temporal aggregation to add value.
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We evaluate stagnation detection across four axes: in-domain accuracy, cross-agent transfer, robustness to design choices, and temporal dynamics of labeling functions.
5	All reported metrics are evaluated against silver labels derived from majority vote over three labeling functions (\S\ref{sec:method}).
6	
7	\paragraph{Circular evaluation caveat.}
8	Structural features (command repetition ratios, file operation counts, edit distances) are computed from the same signals that the labeling functions use to produce silver labels.
9	Consequently, the in-domain structural F1 of 0.9951 reflects an upper bound on how well these features can \emph{reverse-engineer} the labeling functions, not detection accuracy against true ground truth.
10	The cross-agent evaluation on OpenHands (0.967 macro-F1) is non-circular: models trained on SWE-Agent LF distributions are tested on a different agent whose LF firing patterns differ substantially (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).
11	A human-annotated gold set provides the definitive non-circular evaluation (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}).
12	
13	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
14	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
15	\label{sec:setup}
16	
17	\paragraph{Datasets.}
18	We extract sliding windows of $k{=}5$ consecutive actions from agent trajectories.
19	\textbf{SWE-Agent} trajectories from SWE-bench \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent} yield 54,809 windows with a stagnation ratio of 28.5\%.
20	\textbf{OpenHands} (OH) trajectories \citep{wang2025openhands} yield 150,652 windows with a stagnation ratio of 6.6\%.
21	Silver labels are produced by majority vote over three labeling functions; confidence equals the number of agreeing LFs (1--3).
22	Unless stated otherwise, evaluation uses the conf${\geq}$2 subset: $N{=}1{,}824$ for SWE-Agent (485 stagnation, 1,339 progress) and $N{=}43{,}376$ for OH.

32	OpenHands & CodeAct   & 150,652 & 6.6 & 43,376 \\

38	
39	\paragraph{Detection methods.}
40	(1)~\textbf{Structural features}: 30 hand-crafted features (repetition rates, file operation counts, edit distances, output entropy) fed to Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), and Gradient Boosting (GB).
41	(2)~\textbf{ProgressProbe}: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B \citep{zhang2025qwen3embedding} embeddings (1024-dim) processed by a 2-layer GRU \citep{cho2014gru} with attention \citep{bahdanau2015attention} (hidden$=$256, dropout$=$0.1), early-stopped at epoch~3 with patience~5.
42	(3)~\textbf{Mean-pool + LR}: Mean-pooled Qwen3 embeddings with logistic regression.
43	(4)~\textbf{LLM-as-Judge}: Claude Sonnet 4.6 zero-shot window-level classification (\$11.66 API cost for the SWE test set).
44	(5)~\textbf{Cosine similarity}: Cosine distance between consecutive window embeddings with a validation-tuned threshold.
45	
46	\paragraph{Metrics.}
47	Macro-F1 is the primary metric. We also report per-class F1 for stagnation (F1\textsubscript{stag}) and progress (F1\textsubscript{prog}).

84	\subsection{Cross-Agent Transfer}
85	\label{sec:cross_agent}

103	\paragraph{Encoder ablation.}
104	Replacing Qwen3-0.6B with BGE-M3 \citep{chen2024bgem3} or E5-large-v2 \citep{wang2024e5} yields probe macro-F1 of 0.9413 and 0.9363, respectively (vs.\ 0.9055 for Qwen3).

106	
107	\paragraph{Window size.}
108	$k{=}5$ is optimal (0.9309 macro-F1); $k{=}3$ drops 5.9\,pp and $k{=}7$ drops 1.8\,pp.
109	Shorter windows lack sufficient context; longer windows dilute signal by spanning both progress and stagnation phases.

111	Details in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:window_ablation}.

113	\paragraph{Data scaling.}
114	Figure~\ref{fig:data_scaling} compares data efficiency across methods.
115	Structural classifiers are extremely data-efficient: RF achieves 0.991 and GB 0.987 at just 10\% training data, fully saturating by 50\%.
116	The probe scales monotonically from 0.805 (10\%) to 0.906 (100\%) but has not plateaued---a 10.1\,pp drop that is roughly 20$\times$ the structural degradation (${\sim}$0.4--0.8\,pp).
117	This data efficiency further supports the structural signal thesis: the features capture patterns so regular that minimal training data suffices.

127	\subsection{Labeling Function Temporal Dynamics}
128	\label{sec:lf_temporal}
129	
130	We analyze when each LF first fires relative to the onset of stagnation episodes (Table~\ref{tab:lf_temporal}, Figure~\ref{fig:lf_temporal}).
131	
132	\begin{table}[t]
133	\centering
134	\small
135	\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
136	\toprule
137	\textbf{LF} & \textbf{Lag} & \textbf{Lead\,\%} & \textbf{Conc.\,\%} & \textbf{Lag\,\%} \\
138	\midrule
139	cmd\_rep      & $-1.87$ & 36.1 & --- & --- \\
140	file\_diff    & $-1.20$ & 17.1 & --- & --- \\
141	outcome\_bp   & $+6.70$ & ---  & --- & 48.4 \\
142	\bottomrule
143	\end{tabular}

146	\end{table}

149	Command repetition leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on average, making it an early warning signal.
150	File diff is near-concurrent ($-1.20$ steps).

152	
153	All pairwise differences are significant (Kruskal-Wallis $H{=}274.3$, $p{=}2.74{\times}10^{-60}$; Bonferroni-corrected pairwise: cmd\_rep vs.\ file\_diff $p{=}1.44{\times}10^{-26}$, cmd\_rep vs.\ outcome\_bp $p{=}6.67{\times}10^{-39}$, file\_diff vs.\ outcome\_bp $p{=}3.47{\times}10^{-47}$).
154	
155	\paragraph{Cross-agent reversal.}
156	On OpenHands, cmd\_rep shifts from leading ($-1.87$) to lagging ($+3.32$ steps).
157	This reversal explains the cmd\_rep pathology analyzed in \S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}: OH's action distribution triggers cmd\_rep on progress windows, inverting its diagnostic value.

164	\end{figure}

167	\subsection{Command Repetition Ablation}
168	\label{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}
169	
170	The cmd\_rep LF votes stagnation on 92.2\% of OH windows (vs.\ 65.5\% on SWE-Agent), with a 71\% false positive rate on OH progress windows.
171	Table~\ref{tab:cmd_rep_ablation} shows the effect of removing it.
172	
173	\begin{table}[t]
174	\centering
175	\small
176	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
177	\toprule
178	\textbf{LF Config} & \textbf{ZS F1} & \textbf{FT F1} & \textbf{FT F1\textsubscript{s}} & \textbf{FT F1\textsubscript{p}} \\
179	\midrule
180	3-LF (w/ cmd\_rep) & 0.530 & 0.751 & 0.544 & 0.959 \\
181	2-LF (no cmd\_rep) & 0.607 & \textbf{0.927} & 0.938 & 0.917 \\
182	\midrule
183	$\Delta$ & +7.7\,pp & +17.6\,pp & +39.4\,pp & $-4.2$\,pp \\
184	\bottomrule
185	\end{tabular}
186	\caption{Effect of removing cmd\_rep on OpenHands probe performance. ZS = zero-shot transfer from SWE-Agent; FT = fine-tuned on 100\% OH data. F1\textsubscript{s}/F1\textsubscript{p} = stagnation/progress F1.}
187	\label{tab:cmd_rep_ablation}
188	\end{table}
189	
190	Removing cmd\_rep improves zero-shot transfer by 7.7\,pp and fine-tuned performance by 17.6\,pp.
191	The gain is driven almost entirely by stagnation recall (+39.4\,pp F1\textsubscript{stag}), at a modest cost to progress detection ($-4.2$\,pp F1\textsubscript{prog}).
192	The 3-LF fine-tuned model's stagnation F1 of 0.544 reveals that cmd\_rep corrupts silver labels so thoroughly that even full fine-tuning on OH data cannot recover.
193	Note that removing cmd\_rep also reduces training data from 101,713 to 72,554 windows (28.5\% reduction); however, the model trained on \emph{less} data with cleaner labels decisively outperforms the model trained on \emph{more} data with corrupted labels, indicating that label quality rather than data volume drives the improvement.
194	This motivates agent-specific LF selection: labeling functions validated on one agent architecture may become adversarial on another.
195	Appendix Table~\ref{tab:cross_agent_cmdrep} extends this analysis to structural zero-shot transfer, where removing cmd\_rep has the opposite effect ($-4.2$\,pp), revealing that the fix requires learned adaptation rather than simple LF deletion.
196	
197	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
198	\subsection{Temporal Label Models}
199	\label{sec:temporal_label_models}
200	
201	We investigate whether incorporating LF temporal dynamics into label aggregation improves over majority vote (MV).
202	Table~\ref{tab:temporal_models} compares three temporal label models \citep{ratner2017snorkel,safranchik2020linkedhmm}.
203	
204	\begin{table}[t]
205	\centering
206	\small
207	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
208	\toprule
209	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Conf${\geq}$2 F1} & \textbf{MV Agr.} & \textbf{Probe F1$^\ddagger$} \\
210	\midrule
211	MV (baseline) & 0.8946$^\ast$ & 1.000 & 0.8468 \\
212	TWV ($\sigma{=}2$) & \textbf{0.9003} & 0.885 & 0.8211 \\
213	Lag-HMM & 0.8936 & 0.820 & --- \\
214	HMM & 0.7502 & 0.685 & 0.6564 \\
215	\bottomrule
216	\end{tabular}
217	\caption{Temporal label model comparison. $^\ast$MV conf${\geq}$2 F1 is a self-evaluation baseline (MV evaluated against itself on high-confidence windows). $^\ddagger$Downstream: probe trained on each method's labels, evaluated on the full SWE-Agent test set ($N{=}8{,}101$) against MV labels.}
218	\label{tab:temporal_models}
219	\end{table}
220	
221	TWV achieves the highest conf${\geq}$2 F1 (0.9003, +0.57\,pp over MV), but this gain does not propagate downstream: a probe trained on TWV labels scores 0.8211 vs.\ 0.8468 for MV-trained ($-2.57$\,pp).
222	TWV flips 14.1\% of conf$=$1 labels, introducing noise that hurts probe training.
223	HMM overpredicts stagnation (29,176 stagnation vs.\ 25,633 progress windows), degrading downstream performance to 0.6564.
224	Lag-HMM closely tracks MV ($-0.1$\,pp) despite explicitly modeling temporal offsets, suggesting that the temporal structure captured by individual LFs does not improve \emph{aggregation}.
225	
226	\paragraph{TWV sensitivity.}
227	The Gaussian kernel bandwidth $\sigma$ is critical: $\sigma{=}2$ is optimal (0.9003); $\sigma{=}1$ drops to 0.8105 and $\sigma{=}5$ drops to 0.808.
228	This narrow operating range, combined with the downstream degradation, makes TWV impractical as a drop-in MV replacement.
229	
230	These results constitute a negative finding: despite clear temporal structure in LF firing patterns (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}), temporal label models do not improve over simple majority vote for downstream stagnation detection.

7	The structural RF's 0.9951 macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:main_results}) is a predictable consequence of feature--label overlap, not a detection achievement.

18	\label{sec:why_tlm_fail}

20	Despite clear temporal structure in LF activations (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}), no temporal label model improves downstream detection over majority vote (\S\ref{sec:temporal_label_models}).
21	The root cause is low label conflict in the 3-LF regime: conf${\geq}$2 windows dominate the training set, leaving few ambiguous labels for temporal models to correct.
22	
23	TWV targets only conf${=}1$ windows, flipping 14.1\% of their labels.
24	These flips introduce noise rather than corrections---downstream probe F1 drops by 2.57\,pp relative to MV-trained.
25	HMM overpredicts stagnation (29,176 vs.\ 25,633 progress windows), producing a distorted label distribution that degrades the probe to 0.6564.
26	Lag-HMM, despite explicitly modeling per-LF temporal offsets, tracks MV within 0.1\,pp---the offset information captured by individual LFs (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}) does not translate into better aggregation.
27

34	We analyze errors of the ProgressProbe (GRU) on the SWE-Agent conf${\geq}$2 test set under the stagnation-positive convention (positive = stagnation throughout).
35	The model misclassifies 131 of 1,824 windows (7.2\% error rate): 85 false negatives (predicted progress, actual stagnation; 64.9\% of errors) and 46 false positives (predicted stagnation, actual progress; 35.1\%).
36

38	Missed stagnation windows (FN) are not borderline cases---the model assigns them a mean stagnation probability of only 0.078 (i.e., high progress confidence of 0.922), with 73\% receiving $>$0.9 progress probability.
39	These windows feature agents performing diverse edits and varied commands that mimic progress patterns while making no effective headway, constituting a systematic blind spot.
40	False positives arise when agents repeat specific command patterns during genuine progress.
41	
42	LF conflict is a strong error predictor: 39.7\% of error windows have at least one LF disagreeing, compared to a 31\% base rate.
43	The cmd\_rep LF contributes the highest per-LF error rate (12.75\%).
44	Errors concentrate in trajectory midpoints (10.2\% error rate vs.\ 6.5\% at endpoints), where the boundary between exploration and stagnation is most ambiguous.
45	Error mass is also non-uniform across trajectories: the two highest-error trajectories account for 18.3\% of all misclassifications.
46	
47	\subsection{Outcome Backpropagation as Distant Supervision}
48	\label{sec:ob_analysis}
49	
50	Outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) is a privileged signal that uses task outcome, unavailable at inference time.
51	A 3-seed split-isolated holdout removing $\lambda_3$ yields macro-F1 of $0.770{\pm}0.022$, a 7.7\,pp drop from the 3-LF baseline of 0.847.

56	This suggests that additional real-time LFs targeting the same coverage gaps could replace the privileged outcome signal without sacrificing label quality.

\section{Analysis}
\label{sec:analysis}

\subsection{Circular Evaluation and Its Implications}
\label{sec:circular}

The structural RF's 0.9951 macro-F1 (\S\ref{sec:main_results}) is a predictable consequence of feature--label overlap, not a detection achievement.
The 30 structural features include repetition ratios and file operation counts---the same signals $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ consume to produce silver labels.
This score therefore represents an upper bound on LF reverse-engineering fidelity.

Two evaluation settings break this circularity.
First, cross-agent transfer: GB trained on SWE-Agent LF distributions achieves 0.9674 macro-F1 on OpenHands, where LF firing patterns differ substantially (e.g., cmd\_rep votes stagnation on 92.2\% vs.\ 65.5\% of windows).
The model cannot memorize LF outputs when tested on a different agent's distribution.
Second, a human-annotated gold set (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}) will provide definitive non-circular ground truth.
Until then, all in-domain structural metrics should be interpreted as LF-agreement scores rather than detection accuracy.

\subsection{Why Temporal Label Models Fail}
\label{sec:why_tlm_fail}

Despite clear temporal structure in LF activations (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}), no temporal label model improves downstream detection over majority vote (\S\ref{sec:temporal_label_models}).
The root cause is low label conflict in the 3-LF regime: conf${\geq}$2 windows dominate the training set, leaving few ambiguous labels for temporal models to correct.

TWV targets only conf${=}1$ windows, flipping 14.1\% of their labels.
These flips introduce noise rather than corrections---downstream probe F1 drops by 2.57\,pp relative to MV-trained.
HMM overpredicts stagnation (29,176 vs.\ 25,633 progress windows), producing a distorted label distribution that degrades the probe to 0.6564.
Lag-HMM, despite explicitly modeling per-LF temporal offsets, tracks MV within 0.1\,pp---the offset information captured by individual LFs (\S\ref{sec:lf_temporal}) does not translate into better aggregation.

Three binary LFs produce at most $2^3{=}8$ voting patterns, yielding too little conflict for temporal models to exploit.
A richer LF set ($>$10 functions with higher disagreement rates) would be needed to create the ambiguity where temporal aggregation could add value \citep{ratner2017snorkel}.

\subsection{Error Analysis}
\label{sec:error_analysis}

We analyze errors of the ProgressProbe (GRU) on the SWE-Agent conf${\geq}$2 test set under the stagnation-positive convention (positive = stagnation throughout).
The model misclassifies 131 of 1,824 windows (7.2\% error rate): 85 false negatives (predicted progress, actual stagnation; 64.9\% of errors) and 46 false positives (predicted stagnation, actual progress; 35.1\%).

The recall bottleneck is the dominant failure mode: $P_\text{stag}{=}0.897$ vs.\ $R_\text{stag}{=}0.825$.
Missed stagnation windows (FN) are not borderline cases---the model assigns them a mean stagnation probability of only 0.078 (i.e., high progress confidence of 0.922), with 73\% receiving $>$0.9 progress probability.
These windows feature agents performing diverse edits and varied commands that mimic progress patterns while making no effective headway, constituting a systematic blind spot.
False positives arise when agents repeat specific command patterns during genuine progress.

LF conflict is a strong error predictor: 39.7\% of error windows have at least one LF disagreeing, compared to a 31\% base rate.
The cmd\_rep LF contributes the highest per-LF error rate (12.75\%).
Errors concentrate in trajectory midpoints (10.2\% error rate vs.\ 6.5\% at endpoints), where the boundary between exploration and stagnation is most ambiguous.
Error mass is also non-uniform across trajectories: the two highest-error trajectories account for 18.3\% of all misclassifications.

\subsection{Outcome Backpropagation as Distant Supervision}
\label{sec:ob_analysis}

Outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) is a privileged signal that uses task outcome, unavailable at inference time.
A 3-seed split-isolated holdout removing $\lambda_3$ yields macro-F1 of $0.770{\pm}0.022$, a 7.7\,pp drop from the 3-LF baseline of 0.847.
$\lambda_3$ contributes 33.5\% of conf${\geq}$2 labels (5,158 of 15,401 windows).

However, $\lambda_3$ functions as a coverage expander rather than an independent corrector: across 43,402 windows where both 2-LF and 3-LF configurations produce labels, their agreement is 100\%.
$\lambda_3$ never flips a majority vote---it only promotes conf${=}1$ windows to conf${=}2$ by adding a third agreeing vote.
This suggests that additional real-time LFs targeting the same coverage gaps could replace the privileged outcome signal without sacrificing label quality.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic study of progress stagnation detection in LLM coding agents, comparing structural features, neural embedding probes, and LLM-as-judge approaches.
Three findings emerge.

First, stagnation signals are fundamentally structural.
Thirty lightweight features achieve 0.9951 in-domain and 0.9674 cross-agent macro-F1, surpassing neural probes (0.9055) and LLM judges (0.6625) by wide margins.
These features are also data-efficient, maintaining F1 above 0.987 with only 10\% of training data.

Second, labeling functions exhibit agent-specific temporal dynamics.
Command repetition leads stagnation onset by 1.87 steps on SWE-Agent but reverses on OpenHands, where its high false-positive rate corrupts silver labels---removing it improves fine-tuned probe F1 by 17.6\,pp.

Third, temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote.
Three temporal aggregation methods---TWV, HMM, and lag-aware HMM---all underperform majority vote, constrained by insufficient inter-LF conflict among three binary labeling functions.

Agent monitoring should therefore prioritize lightweight structural features ({<}5\,ms per window, no GPU) over embedding or LLM approaches.
The circular evaluation caveat applies to in-domain results; cross-agent transfer provides stronger validation.

Future work includes extending evaluation to non-software-engineering agent domains, online integration with early termination or strategy switching, scaling to {>}10 labeling functions to test whether temporal aggregation becomes useful, and validation against the pending 650-window gold set.

Our central finding is that structural features dominate zero-shot cross-agent transfer: 30 features---command repetition rates, file operation counts, edit distances---achieve RF 0.9951 in-domain and GB 0.9674 cross-agent macro-F1 with zero target data, surpassing the neural probe's zero-shot transfer (0.598) and LLM-as-judge (0.6625) by +36.9\,pp and +30.5\,pp, respectively. The probe rapidly closes this gap with modest fine-tuning (0.976 at 100\% OH data, within 2.2\,pp of structural). In-domain evaluation reflects circular agreement with LF-derived silver labels; cross-agent transfer and a pending gold set provide non-circular validation.

\label{sec:circular}

\label{sec:conclusion}

6	\citet{orlanski2026slopcodebench} document this degradation on SlopCodeBench, recording verbosity increases of 77\% and quality drops of 75.5\% in long-horizon coding trajectories, with no agent fully solving any benchmark problem end-to-end.
7	Crucially, the dominant failure pattern is not simple repetition but what we term \emph{semantic stagnation}: the agent issues varied commands, edits different files, and generates plausible-looking outputs, yet its behavior is functionally stuck.
8	This ``looks busy but going in circles'' pattern defeats existing monitoring tools, because surface-level action diversity masks the underlying lack of progress.
9	We observe this phenomenon at scale: across trajectories from two architecturally distinct agents---SWE-Agent \citep{yang2024sweagent} and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands}---on SWE-bench tasks \citep{jimenez2024swebench}, 28.5\% and 21.45\% of sliding windows exhibit stagnation under our silver labeling scheme, respectively, confirming that the failure mode is both prevalent and highly agent-dependent.
10	
11	Existing approaches address aspects of this problem but fall short in three ways.
12	First, \emph{repetition detectors} such as cycle detection \citep{george2025cycledetection} and SpecRA \citep{pipis2025reasoningloop} identify structural repetition---exact or near-exact loops in action sequences---but by design miss semantically diverse stagnation where the agent varies its surface behavior while remaining functionally stuck.
13	Second, \emph{step-level scoring} via process reward models \citep{xi2025agentprm} evaluates individual actions in isolation, discarding the window-level temporal dynamics that distinguish transient setbacks from sustained stagnation---a distinction that requires reasoning over sequences of consecutive actions \citep{chen2025monitoring}.
14	A sequence of failed commands followed by a strategy switch, for instance, carries different diagnostic information than the same commands evaluated independently.
15	Third, \emph{LLM self-evaluation} \citep{shinn2023reflexion} is both expensive and fundamentally limited by the stuck model's own judgment; our LLM-as-judge baseline achieves only 0.6625 macro-F1 at \$11.66 per test set, well below lightweight feature-based alternatives.
16	More fundamentally, none of these approaches asks the prior question: \emph{what signals actually carry stagnation information?}
17	No systematic study has investigated whether detecting subtle agent failure requires sophisticated semantic understanding or whether simpler structural patterns suffice.
18	
19	We address this question through a systematic empirical study (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
20	Using a weak supervision framework \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming,ratner2017snorkel}, we construct silver-labeled datasets from over 205K windows spanning SWE-Agent (54,809 windows, 28.5\% silver-labeled stagnation) and OpenHands (150,652 windows, 21.45\% stagnation).
21	Three labeling functions provide complementary noisy votes: command repetition ($\lambda_1$) targets repetitive behavior, file diff delta ($\lambda_2$) targets output productivity, and outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) propagates task-level outcomes backward through the trajectory.
22	Majority vote aggregation produces window-level binary labels with confidence scores.
23	Our window-level formulation ($k{=}5$ consecutive actions, stride 1) captures short-range temporal patterns---such as repeated failures followed by strategy changes---that step-level approaches cannot express, while providing the granularity to pinpoint \emph{when} stagnation begins and ends within a trajectory, enabling targeted interventions.

As these deployments scale, a critical failure mode has emerged that is qualitatively different from crashes or syntax errors: the agent \emph{stagnates}---continuing to produce actions that appear purposeful while making no meaningful progress toward the task goal.
\citet{orlanski2026slopcodebench} document this degradation on SlopCodeBench, recording verbosity increases of 77\% and quality drops of 75.5\% in long-horizon coding trajectories, with no agent fully solving any benchmark problem end-to-end.
Crucially, the dominant failure pattern is not simple repetition but what we term \emph{semantic stagnation}: the agent issues varied commands, edits different files, and generates plausible-looking outputs, yet its behavior is functionally stuck.
This ``looks busy but going in circles'' pattern defeats existing monitoring tools, because surface-level action diversity masks the underlying lack of progress.
We observe this phenomenon at scale: across trajectories from two architecturally distinct agents---SWE-Agent \citep{yang2024sweagent} and OpenHands \citep{wang2025openhands}---on SWE-bench tasks \citep{jimenez2024swebench}, 28.5\% and 21.45\% of sliding windows exhibit stagnation under our silver labeling scheme, respectively, confirming that the failure mode is both prevalent and highly agent-dependent.

Existing approaches address aspects of this problem but fall short in three ways.
First, \emph{repetition detectors} such as cycle detection \citep{george2025cycledetection} and SpecRA \citep{pipis2025reasoningloop} identify structural repetition---exact or near-exact loops in action sequences---but by design miss semantically diverse stagnation where the agent varies its surface behavior while remaining functionally stuck.
Second, \emph{step-level scoring} via process reward models \citep{xi2025agentprm} evaluates individual actions in isolation, discarding the window-level temporal dynamics that distinguish transient setbacks from sustained stagnation---a distinction that requires reasoning over sequences of consecutive actions \citep{chen2025monitoring}.
A sequence of failed commands followed by a strategy switch, for instance, carries different diagnostic information than the same commands evaluated independently.
Third, \emph{LLM self-evaluation} \citep{shinn2023reflexion} is both expensive and fundamentally limited by the stuck model's own judgment; our LLM-as-judge baseline achieves only 0.6625 macro-F1 at \$11.66 per test set, well below lightweight feature-based alternatives.
More fundamentally, none of these approaches asks the prior question: \emph{what signals actually carry stagnation information?}
No systematic study has investigated whether detecting subtle agent failure requires sophisticated semantic understanding or whether simpler structural patterns suffice.

We address this question through a systematic empirical study (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
Using a weak supervision framework \citep{ratner2016dataprogramming,ratner2017snorkel}, we construct silver-labeled datasets from over 205K windows spanning SWE-Agent (54,809 windows, 28.5\% silver-labeled stagnation) and OpenHands (150,652 windows, 21.45\% stagnation).
Three labeling functions provide complementary noisy votes: command repetition ($\lambda_1$) targets repetitive behavior, file diff delta ($\lambda_2$) targets output productivity, and outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$) propagates task-level outcomes backward through the trajectory.
Majority vote aggregation produces window-level binary labels with confidence scores.
Our window-level formulation ($k{=}5$ consecutive actions, stride 1) captures short-range temporal patterns---such as repeated failures followed by strategy changes---that step-level approaches cannot express, while providing the granularity to pinpoint \emph{when} stagnation begins and ends within a trajectory, enabling targeted interventions.
Against these silver labels, we systematically compare hand-crafted structural features, a neural embedding probe, and an LLM-as-judge baseline.

Our study yields three principal findings.

\textbf{Finding 1: Structural features dominate zero-shot cross-agent transfer.}
Thirty hand-crafted features---command repetition rates, file operation counts, edit distances---achieve 0.9951 macro-F1 in-domain (Random Forest) and 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1 (Gradient Boosting, SWE-Agent $\to$ OpenHands) with zero target data, outperforming the GRU embedding probe \citep{cho2014gru} zero-shot (0.598 on OpenHands, near chance) and the LLM-as-judge baseline (0.6625) by +36.9\,pp and +30.5\,pp, respectively.
However, with 100\% target fine-tuning the probe reaches 0.976 macro-F1, surpassing the structural baseline (0.967)---demonstrating that probe representations recover cross-agent generalization with sufficient adaptation data.
We note that in-domain evaluation uses silver labels (\S\ref{sec:circular}); cross-agent transfer and a pending gold set (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}) provide non-circular validation.
The structural advantage is encoder-agnostic: three embedding backbones \citep{zhang2025qwen3embedding} all yield probe F1 above 0.90, confirming that the probe's temporal architecture rather than a specific pretrained encoder drives performance.
The in-domain score of 0.9951 reflects circular evaluation---structural features overlap with LF inputs---but the cross-agent score of 0.967, where models trained on one agent's LF distribution are tested on another with substantially different firing patterns, breaks this circularity.
This finding challenges the prevailing intuition that detecting subtle agent failures requires complex language understanding, and suggests that lightweight structural monitoring---no GPU, under 5\,ms per window---may be more practical than neural or LLM-based approaches for real-time agent oversight.

\textbf{Finding 2: Label quality, not LF selection, is the dominant cross-agent transfer bottleneck.}
Labeling functions exhibit systematic temporal dynamics that reverse across agents: command repetition ($\lambda_1$) leads stagnation onset on SWE-Agent by $-1.87$ steps but lags on OpenHands by $+3.32$ steps.
A label quality audit reveals that fixing OH label version bias---correcting stagnation rate from 6.56\% to 21.45\%---improves 5\% fine-tuning F1 from 0.570 (under previous label version) to 0.850.
Prevalence-matched ablation shows that $\lambda_1$'s core value is coverage ($-29.4$\,pp when removed, $p \approx 0$), not label precision: it fires on only 5.39\% of OH windows with precision 97.91\% (FP rate 2.3\%).

\textbf{Finding 3: Temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote.}
Three temporal label models---time-varying weights (TWV), Hidden Markov Models \citep{safranchik2020linkedhmm}, and lag-aware HMMs---all fail to surpass majority vote on downstream detection.
TWV achieves marginally higher self-evaluated F1 but degrades downstream probe performance by 2.57\,pp.
The root cause: three binary LFs produce too little inter-LF conflict for temporal aggregation to exploit.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Structural signal discovery.} We demonstrate that 30 lightweight structural features achieve near-perfect stagnation detection (0.9951 in-domain, 0.967 cross-agent macro-F1) with zero target data, outperforming the probe zero-shot (+36.9\,pp) and LLM-as-judge (+30.5\,pp), with no GPU and under 5\,ms per window. The probe closes the gap to within 2\,pp with $\leq$20\% target data, delineating when structural monitoring suffices and when fine-tuning is warranted.
    \item \textbf{Label quality as transfer bottleneck.} We show that labeling functions exhibit agent-specific temporal reversals and that fixing label version bias (stag rate 6.56\%$\to$21.45\%) dominates LF selection for cross-agent transfer, informing future weak-supervision design on sequential agent data.
    \item \textbf{Temporal label model negative finding.} We show that three temporal label models fail to improve over majority vote for downstream detection, despite clear temporal structure in LF firing patterns. This constrains future temporal label model research: the 3-LF regime produces insufficient conflict for temporal aggregation to add value.
\end{enumerate}

35	\subsubsection{Labeling Functions}
36	\label{sec:labeling_functions}
37	
38	We design three LFs that target complementary signals of stagnation (Table~\ref{tab:lf_design}).
39	
40	\paragraph{Command repetition ($\lambda_1$).}
41	Computes the proportion of repeated commands within window $w_i$.
42	A high repetition ratio triggers a stagnation vote, capturing overt repetitive behavior such as re-running failing commands.
43	This LF never abstains: it votes stagnation when the repetition ratio exceeds a threshold and progress otherwise.
44	It votes stagnation on 65.5\% of SWE-Agent windows and 92.2\% of OpenHands windows; the elevated OH rate reflects differences in action distributions across agent architectures (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).
45	
46	\paragraph{File diff delta ($\lambda_2$).}
47	Measures the fraction of steps within $w_i$ that produce code modifications (file creates, edits, or deletes).
48	A low modification frequency triggers a stagnation vote; windows with more than one edited file receive a progress vote; windows with exactly one or zero edits abstain ($\bot$).
49	On OpenHands, this LF achieves 87\% correctness on progress windows, making it the most reliable cross-agent signal.
50	
51	\paragraph{Outcome backpropagation ($\lambda_3$).}
52	Uses the final task outcome (resolved/unresolved) as distant supervision.
53	For unresolved tasks, the last two windows and any windows following a timeout or stuck signal receive stagnation votes; resolved tasks receive progress votes in the corresponding windows.
54	All other windows abstain ($\bot$).
55	Unlike $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, which operate on local window content, $\lambda_3$ propagates a global signal backward through time.
56	This makes it a form of distant supervision: individually noisy, but complementary to the real-time signals when aggregated.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	We evaluate stagnation detection across four axes: in-domain accuracy, cross-agent transfer, robustness to design choices, and temporal dynamics of labeling functions.
5	All reported metrics are evaluated against silver labels derived from majority vote over three labeling functions (\S\ref{sec:method}).
6	
7	\paragraph{Circular evaluation caveat.}
8	Structural features (command repetition ratios, file operation counts, edit distances) are computed from the same signals that the labeling functions use to produce silver labels.
9	Consequently, the in-domain structural F1 of 0.9951 reflects an upper bound on how well these features can \emph{reverse-engineer} the labeling functions, not detection accuracy against true ground truth.
10	The cross-agent evaluation on OpenHands (0.967 macro-F1) is non-circular: models trained on SWE-Agent LF distributions are tested on a different agent whose LF firing patterns differ substantially (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).
11	A human-annotated gold set provides the definitive non-circular evaluation (\S\ref{sec:gold_set}).
12	
13	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
14	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
15	\label{sec:setup}
16	
17	\paragraph{Datasets.}
18	We extract sliding windows of $k{=}5$ consecutive actions from agent trajectories.
19	\textbf{SWE-Agent} trajectories from SWE-bench \citep{jimenez2024swebench,yang2024sweagent} yield 54,809 windows with a stagnation ratio of 28.5\%.
20	\textbf{OpenHands} (OH) trajectories \citep{wang2025openhands} yield 150,652 windows with a stagnation ratio of 21.4\%.
21	Silver labels are produced by majority vote over three labeling functions; confidence equals the number of agreeing LFs (1--3).
22	Unless stated otherwise, evaluation uses the conf${\geq}$2 subset: $N{=}1{,}824$ for SWE-Agent (485 stagnation, 1,339 progress) and $N{=}43{,}376$ for OH.
23	
24	\begin{table}[t]
25	\centering
26	\small
27	\begin{tabular}{llrrc}
28	\toprule
29	\textbf{Agent} & \textbf{Source} & \textbf{Windows} & \textbf{Stag\,\%} & \textbf{Conf${\geq}$2} \\
30	\midrule
31	SWE-Agent & SWE-bench & 54,809 & 28.5 & 15,401 \\
32	OpenHands & CodeAct   & 150,652 & 21.4 & 43,376 \\
33	\bottomrule
34	\end{tabular}
35	\caption{Dataset statistics. Stagnation ratios differ substantially across agents, reflecting different action distributions.}
36	\label{tab:dataset_stats}
37	\end{table}
38	
39	\paragraph{Detection methods.}
40	(1)~\textbf{Structural features}: 30 hand-crafted features (repetition rates, file operation counts, edit distances, output entropy) fed to Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), and Gradient Boosting (GB).
41	(2)~\textbf{ProgressProbe}: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B \citep{zhang2025qwen3embedding} embeddings (1024-dim) processed by a 2-layer GRU \citep{cho2014gru} with attention \citep{bahdanau2015attention} (hidden$=$256, dropout$=$0.1), early-stopped at epoch~3 with patience~5.
42	(3)~\textbf{Mean-pool + LR}: Mean-pooled Qwen3 embeddings with logistic regression.
43	(4)~\textbf{LLM-as-Judge}: Claude Sonnet 4.6 zero-shot window-level classification (\$11.66 API cost for the SWE test set).
44	(5)~\textbf{Cosine similarity}: Cosine distance between consecutive window embeddings with a validation-tuned threshold.
45	
46	\paragraph{Metrics.}
47	Macro-F1 is the primary metric. We also report per-class F1 for stagnation (F1\textsubscript{stag}) and progress (F1\textsubscript{prog}).
48	
49	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
50	\subsection{Main Results}
51	\label{sec:main_results}
52	
53	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents in-domain results on the SWE-Agent conf${\geq}$2 test set and cross-agent transfer to OpenHands.
54

56	\centering
57	\small

60	& \multicolumn{3}{c}{\textbf{SWE-Agent In-Domain} (conf${\geq}$2)} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{OpenHands Transfer}} \\
61	\cmidrule(lr){2-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6}

66	Structural LR$^\dagger$       & 0.9874 & 0.9815 & 0.9933 & 0.7801 & 0.9671 \\

Best in \textbf{bold}, second-best \underline{underlined}.}
75	\label{tab:main_results}

77	
78	In-domain, structural RF achieves 0.9951 macro-F1, exceeding the GRU probe by 8.96 percentage points (pp) and the LLM judge by 33.3\,pp.
79	However, the structural--probe gap is inflated by circular evaluation: structural features reconstruct the LFs that generated the labels.
80	The more informative comparison is among non-circular methods: the GRU probe outperforms mean-pool~+~LR by 6.2\,pp, confirming that temporal modeling within windows adds value beyond static embedding aggregation.
81	The LLM judge underperforms all learned methods despite substantially higher cost.
82	
83	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
84	\subsection{Cross-Agent Transfer}
85	\label{sec:cross_agent}
86	
87	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} (right columns) shows models trained on SWE-Agent and evaluated on OpenHands without any OH training data.
88	Structural GB transfers best, achieving 0.967 macro-F1 on all OH windows.
89	RF drops to 0.912 on all-confidence OH data despite matching GB in-domain, suggesting GB's boosted ensemble is more robust to distributional shift.
90	Both structural models recover to $>$0.99 on conf${\geq}$2 OH windows, where label noise is lower.
91	
92	The probe's zero-shot transfer (0.598 on all windows) lags structural GB by 36.9\,pp, but full OH fine-tuning closes this gap dramatically: the fine-tuned probe reaches 0.9763, within 2.2\,pp of structural GB (0.967) on the same test set (\S\ref{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}).
93	The asymmetry between structural and learned methods is thus stage-dependent: in the zero-data regime, structural features transfer naturally while learned embeddings do not (+36.9\,pp gap); with target-domain labels, the probe converges to near-structural performance.
94	The practical implication is a deployment trade-off: use structural features when no labeled data is available; invest in probe fine-tuning when annotation budget permits.
95	
96	\paragraph{Multi-seed stability.}
97	Structural RF: $0.9951{\pm}0.0000$ in-domain (3 seeds, zero variance); GB cross-agent: $0.9678{\pm}0.0015$.
98	The probe shows higher variance: $0.9185{\pm}0.0113$, though all seeds exceed 0.90.
99	
100	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
101	\subsection{Robustness Analysis}
102	\label{sec:robustness}
103	
104	\paragraph{Encoder ablation.}
105	Replacing Qwen3-0.6B with BGE-M3 \citep{chen2024bgem3} or E5-large-v2 \citep{wang2024e5} yields probe macro-F1 of 0.9413 and 0.9363, respectively (vs.\ 0.9055 for Qwen3).
106	All encoders exceed 0.90, indicating the probe's temporal architecture, not a specific encoder, drives performance. Full results appear in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:encoder_ablation}.
107	
108	\paragraph{Window size.}
109	$k{=}5$ is optimal (0.9309 macro-F1); $k{=}3$ drops 5.9\,pp and $k{=}7$ drops 1.8\,pp.
110	Shorter windows lack sufficient context; longer windows dilute signal by spanning both progress and stagnation phases.
111	The 0.9309 figure differs from the main table's 0.9055 because the window ablation uses a separate train/val/test split (seed~42, Qwen3-0.6B encoder) to enable controlled comparison across window sizes; cross-split variance accounts for the gap.
112	Details in Appendix Table~\ref{tab:window_ablation}.
113	
114	\paragraph{Data scaling.}
115	Figure~\ref{fig:data_scaling} compares data efficiency across methods.
116	Structural classifiers are extremely data-efficient: RF achieves 0.991 and GB 0.987 at just 10\% training data, fully saturating by 50\%.
117	The probe scales monotonically from 0.805 (10\%) to 0.906 (100\%) but has not plateaued---a 10.1\,pp drop that is roughly 20$\times$ the structural degradation (${\sim}$0.4--0.8\,pp).
118	This data efficiency further supports the structural signal thesis: the features capture patterns so regular that minimal training data suffices.
119	
120	\begin{figure}[t]
121	\centering
122	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{../../figures/paper/fig_data_scaling.pdf}
123	\caption{Macro-F1 vs.\ training data fraction. Structural classifiers (RF, GB) saturate by 50\% data; the probe scales monotonically but remains 9\,pp below at 100\%.}
124	\label{fig:data_scaling}
125	\end{figure}
126	
127	%-------------------------------------------------------------------
128	\subsection{Labeling Function Temporal Dynamics}
129	\label{sec:lf_temporal}
130	
131	We analyze when each LF first fires relative to the onset of stagnation episodes (Table~\ref{tab:lf_temporal}, Figure~\ref{fig:lf_temporal}).
132	
133	\begin{table}[t]
134	\centering
135	\small
136	\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
137	\toprule
138	\textbf{LF} & \textbf{Lag} & \textbf{Lead\,\%} & \textbf{Conc.\,\%} & \textbf{Lag\,\%} \\

168	\subsection{Label Quality and cmd\_rep Coverage}
169	\label{sec:cmd_rep_ablation}
170	
171	A label quality audit revealed that the OH embedding vectors used for silver labeling contained a version mismatch, causing systematic label errors.
172	After correction, the OH stagnation rate shifted from 6.56\% to 21.45\%, with 21,898 window labels flipping.
173	This section quantifies how label quality and cmd\_rep coverage jointly affect probe transfer.
174	
175	\paragraph{Label correction impact on probe transfer.}
176	With corrected labels, the 3-LF probe improves from zero-shot 0.598 to fine-tuned 0.9763 (previously 0.751 under corrupted labels).
177	The improvement is most dramatic at low data fractions: 5\% fine-tuning now reaches 0.850, exceeding the old 50\% result (0.688) by 16.2\,pp.
178	Label quality, not model capacity, was the transfer bottleneck.
179	
180	\paragraph{Prevalence-matched ablation.}

182

184	\centering
185	\small
186	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
187	\toprule
188	\textbf{LF Config} & \textbf{Macro-F1} & \textbf{F1\textsubscript{stag}} & \textbf{F1\textsubscript{prog}} \\

190	3-LF (w/ cmd\_rep) & \textbf{0.9763} & 0.960 & 0.993 \\
191	2-LF (no cmd\_rep) & 0.6822 & 0.481 & 0.884 \\
192	\midrule
193	$\Delta$ & $-29.4$\,pp & $-47.9$\,pp & $-10.9$\,pp \\
194	\bottomrule
195	\end{tabular}

197	\label{tab:cmd_rep_ablation}
198	\end{table}

200	Removing cmd\_rep drops macro-F1 by 29.4\,pp (McNemar $\chi^2{=}1551$, $p{\approx}0$), a statistically significant degradation driven primarily by stagnation recall ($-47.9$\,pp F1\textsubscript{stag}).
201	
202	\paragraph{Coverage, not label quality, explains the gap.}
203	The 29.4\,pp drop is not caused by cmd\_rep improving label accuracy.
204	After correction, cmd\_rep fires on only 5.39\% of OH windows (down from the previously reported 92.2\% under corrupted embeddings) with 97.91\% precision---a high-precision, low-recall signal.
205	On the 4,070 windows where both 2-LF and 3-LF labels are defined, the two configurations agree on 100\% of labels: cmd\_rep does not change any label where the other two LFs already vote.
206	Its contribution is purely \emph{coverage}: including cmd\_rep expands the training set from ${\sim}$4K to ${\sim}$43K windows (a ${\sim}$10$\times$ increase).
207	The 2-LF model's low F1 reflects data volume collapse---too few training examples to learn the stagnation distribution---rather than label corruption.
208	
209	\paragraph{Implications for weak supervision.}
210	These results reframe how labeling functions contribute to weak supervision pipelines.
211	A high-precision, low-recall LF like cmd\_rep may appear redundant when its labels are a subset of the majority vote, yet removing it causes training data to collapse by an order of magnitude.
212	In prevalence-matched evaluation, this data reduction manifests as a 29.4\,pp F1 drop.
213	The core contribution of such LFs is coverage provision, not label refinement: they extend the labelable portion of the input space rather than correcting other LFs' errors.
214

216	\subsection{Temporal Label Models}
217	\label{sec:temporal_label_models}
218	
219	We investigate whether incorporating LF temporal dynamics into label aggregation improves over majority vote (MV).
220	Table~\ref{tab:temporal_models} compares three temporal label models \citep{ratner2017snorkel,safranchik2020linkedhmm}.
221	
222	\begin{table}[t]
223	\centering
224	\small
225	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
226	\toprule
227	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Conf${\geq}$2 F1} & \textbf{MV Agr.} & \textbf{Probe F1$^\ddagger$} \\
228	\midrule

230	TWV ($\sigma{=}2$) & \textbf{0.9003} & 0.885 & 0.8211 \\

232	HMM & 0.7502 & 0.685 & 0.6564 \\
233	\bottomrule
234	\end{tabular}

236	\label{tab:temporal_models}
237	\end{table}
238	
239	TWV achieves the highest conf${\geq}$2 F1 (0.9003, +0.57\,pp over MV), but this gain does not propagate downstream: a probe trained on TWV labels scores 0.8211 vs.\ 0.8468 for MV-trained ($-2.57$\,pp).
240	TWV flips 14.1\% of conf$=$1 labels, introducing noise that hurts probe training.
241	HMM overpredicts stagnation (29,176 stagnation vs.\ 25,633 progress windows), degrading downstream performance to 0.6564.
242	Lag-HMM closely tracks MV ($-0.1$\,pp) despite explicitly modeling temporal offsets, suggesting that the temporal structure captured by individual LFs does not improve \emph{aggregation}.
243	
244	\paragraph{TWV sensitivity.}
245	The Gaussian kernel bandwidth $\sigma$ is critical: $\sigma{=}2$ is optimal (0.9003); $\sigma{=}1$ drops to 0.8105 and $\sigma{=}5$ drops to 0.808.
246	This narrow operating range, combined with the downstream degradation, makes TWV impractical as a drop-in MV replacement.
247
